sections.heading: Conectores básicos en inglés
sections.body: Los conectores lógicos (*linking words*) articulan el flujo de las ideas en una conversación o texto, indicando si una idea complementa a otra, la contradice, o explica su causa o consecuencia.

sections.heading: And & Or: Adición y Opción
sections.body: **'And'** une dos elementos o proposiciones de igual peso (*'I like coffee and tea'*). **'Or'** se utiliza para presentar alternativas o posibilidades (*'Do you want tea or coffee?'*).

sections.heading: But: Contraste
sections.body: **'But'** introduce un contraste, matiz o resultado inesperado (*'I was tired, but I finished the report'*). Cuando une dos oraciones completas independientes, suele llevar una coma antes de *but*.

sections.heading: So: Consecuencia y resultado
sections.body: **'So'** conecta una causa con su efecto o resultado directo (*'It was raining, so we stayed home'*). Equivale a 'por lo tanto' o 'así que' en español.

sections.heading: Because vs. Because of: Causa o motivo
sections.body: **'Because'** introduce una subordinada con sujeto y verbo (*'She studied hard because she wanted to pass'*). En contraste, **'because of'** es una preposición compuesta que siempre va seguida de un sustantivo, pronombre o sintagma nominal (*'We cancelled the game because of the rain'*).

sections.heading: Regla de puntuación: La coma con conjunciones
sections.body: Cuando unes dos cláusulas independientes completas (cada una con su propio sujeto y verbo) usando *and*, *but*, *or* o *so*, coloca una **coma antes del conector**: *'She loves reading, but her brother prefers movies.'*

examples.english: I was tired, but I finished the report.
It rained heavily, so we cancelled the outdoor trip.
She succeeded because she worked consistently.
The flight was delayed because of the dense fog.
Do you want to eat at home, or should we order food?
examples.note: 'Or' ofreciendo una alternativa entre dos cláusulas.

exercises.instruction: Completa cada oración con el conector adecuado.
items: I was tired, ___ I went to bed early. (so / although)
___ it was raining, we went for a long walk. (Although / Because)
She studied hard ___ she passed the exam with top marks. (and / but)
He didn't call ___ he forgot his phone at work. (because / however)
We couldn't play tennis ___ the heavy rain. (because / because of)
He wanted to buy the laptop, ___ it was too expensive. (but / so)
Would you like to pay in cash ___ by credit card? (or / and)
She wore a warm coat ___ it was freezing outside. (because / so)

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because' or 'because of' in English?
options: I stayed at home because the heavy rain.
I stayed at home because of it was raining.
I stayed at home because it was raining.
I stayed at home because of I was tired.
quiz.explanation: 'Because' must be followed by a full clause with subject and verb ('it was raining'). 'Because of' is followed only by a noun phrase ('because of the rain').

quiz.question: Choose the sentence with correct punctuation and conjunction usage:
options: I love swimming, but my sister prefers running.
I love swimming, and but my sister prefers running.
I love swimming but, my sister prefers running.
I love swimming, because my sister prefers running.
quiz.explanation: When joining two independent clauses with 'but', the comma goes directly before the coordinating conjunction, without combining 'and' and 'but'.

quiz.question: Which connector best completes the result: 'The traffic was terrible, ___ we arrived late.'?
quiz.explanation: 'So' introduces the consequence or result of the first clause ('traffic was terrible' -> 'so we arrived late').

quiz.question: Complete correctly: 'The concert was cancelled ___ the storm.'
quiz.explanation: 'The storm' is a noun phrase without a verb, so 'because of' is required instead of 'because'.
